Can a cheque bounce prosecution under Section 138 of the NI Act succeed if the cheque was issued for a time-barred debt? ⚖️
In a significant ruling (Social Leasing (India) Ltd. v. Rajan Kumar Kanthwal, Criminal Appeal No. 116/2011), the Hon’ble High Court of Himachal Pradesh (Justice Rakesh Kainthla) upheld the acquittal of an accused, clarifying the strict intersection between the Limitation Act and Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
For corporate legal counsels, lending institutions, business owners, and litigation practitioners handling commercial recovery, this ruling underscores three critical legal principles:
1. No "Legally Enforceable Debt" After Limitation Expires
Under the Explanation to Section 138 NI Act, a cheque must be drawn for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. In this case, a loan advanced on April 10, 1996, became time-barred after three years. A cheque issued thereafter on October 18, 1999—which returned dishonored with the remark 'Account Closed'—could not attract criminal liability because the underlying debt was no longer legally recoverable on the date the cheque was drawn.
2. Mere Issuance of a Cheque Does Not Revive a Time-Barred Debt
The Court reaffirmed that simply handing over a cheque after the three-year limitation period expires does not automatically revive a dead claim or extend limitation under the Limitation Act.
3. Crucial Statutory Exceptions for Creditors
While a standalone cheque fails, creditors can still protect their recovery rights through two established legal mechanisms:
Section 18, Limitation Act: Obtaining a written acknowledgment of liability before the initial three-year limitation period expires.
Section 25(3), Indian Contract Act, 1872: Executing a distinct, express written promise signed by the debtor to pay a time-barred debt, which creates a fresh, enforceable contract.
Proactive documentation and timely limitation tracking remain the strongest safeguards against commercial bad debts.
